<div class="lead">
The tagging script reads the title and the description of every result reported in PRMS, the CGIAR performance and
results management system. It finds the climate information they contain with the CGIAR climate taxonomy, describes
the climate pathway, and compares what the text says with the climate marker given in PRMS. It applies the CGIAR
Standard for Tagging Climate-Related Work of 10 November 2026. This page explains each part of the script in plain words,
for readers who do not write code.
</div>

# What goes in and what comes out

| | |
|---|---|
| **Goes in** | The PRMS export: for each result its title, description, climate marker (Principal, Significant, Not targeted or none), countries and program. The CGIAR climate taxonomy, version 6 (768 terms). |
| **Two AI models** | gpt-5-mini tags the terms; gpt-5 reads each text with climate information twice, to find the climate measure and the purpose. |
| **Comes out** | Three documents: (1) the tagged results, one row per result, with the tags and links; (2) a diagnosis page to read the run; (3) the taxonomy findings, with a decision column for the taxonomy team. Every record also keeps the AI's answers as received, so that a change to a rule can be replayed later at no cost. |

The AI never sees the PRMS marker, the countries or the program. It sees only the title and the description.

# The steps for one result

<div class="flow">
<div class="step"><span class="n">1</span><b>Prepare</b><br>English text, geography</div>
<div class="step"><span class="n">2</span><b>Term search</b><br>code finds taxonomy terms</div>
<div class="step"><span class="n">3</span><b>Skip</b><br>no climate word: no AI call</div>
<div class="step ai"><span class="n">4</span><b>Tagging</b><br>AI judges each term</div>
<div class="step"><span class="n">5</span><b>Checks</b><br>code checks every answer</div>
<div class="step ai"><span class="n">6</span><b>Reading</b><br>AI, twice: measure and purpose</div>
<div class="step"><span class="n">7</span><b>Decisions</b><br>pathway, level, marker answer</div>
<div class="step"><span class="n">8</span><b>Findings</b><br>gaps in the taxonomy</div>
</div>

<p class="note">Steps in green are done by an AI model. All other steps are done by code, the same way every time.</p>

The sections below follow these steps. Each section says what the step does, why, and where the rules of the standard
are applied. The name in grey at the end of a section is the part of the script that does it, for readers who want to
find it in the code.

# 1. Preparing the text

- The title and the description are joined into one text. Nothing else from PRMS is read by the AI.
- A text in another language is translated into English first. The record says that it was translated.
- **Geography** (standard, Rule 4) is taken from the PRMS Countries field. When the field is empty, the countries named
  in the text are used and marked as taken from the text. When none of the countries named in the text is in the
  field, the result is flagged for review.
- A result with an empty text gets "no comparison".

<p class="where">In the script: parts <code>data</code>, <code>geography</code>, <code>pipeline</code> (make_ctx)</p>

# 2. Finding the taxonomy terms in the text

The code searches the text for every term and synonym of the taxonomy. The terms it finds are the **candidates** that
the AI will judge. The search:

- ignores case and punctuation, and finds plurals and other word forms ("droughts", "drought-tolerant");
- allows one extra word inside a term ("climate-resilient yam varieties" is Climate-resilient variety);
- keeps the most precise term: "climate" inside "climate resilience" is not offered separately;
- **hides known names first**: a climate word inside the name of a programme, project, fund or organisation is not
  climate information on its own (standard, Rule 3). "Livestock and Climate Initiative" or "Green Climate Fund" do not
  make a text climate-related;
- matches **acronyms only in exact capitals**, as whole words, with a plural "s" ("NDCs"). An acronym with another common
  meaning (CSA, CIS, NAP) counts only when the text spells it out or holds climate words. The acronyms come from a
  register: a candidate report with a decision for each acronym (102 accepted). "gaps" is therefore no longer read as
  GAP, Good agricultural practice;
- offers at most 60 candidates per text.

Four terms are applied in a provisional way until the taxonomy team decides (Anticipatory action, Food system
transformation, Green Climate Fund, Avoided deforestation). The taxonomy file itself is not changed by the script.

<p class="where">In the script: parts <code>taxonomy</code>, <code>prefilter</code> (shortlist_ids)</p>

# 3. Skipping texts with no climate information

A text that holds no climate word (climate change, drought, flood, heat, emissions, carbon, methane and similar) and no
stand-alone climate term gets **no AI call**. It is recorded as having no climate information. General terms on their
own, such as farmer, training or irrigation, never give climate information (standard, Rules 2 and 3), so such a text
cannot become climate-related whatever the AI says. On the pilot of 200 results, 132 needed no AI call.

<p class="where">In the script: part <code>pipeline</code> (skip_ai)</p>

# 4. The tagging call (AI)

The AI (gpt-5-mini) receives the text and the list of candidates, with instructions that follow the standard rule by
rule and use the standard's own worked examples. For each candidate it fills a fixed form:

- **kept or not**: is the term used in its taxonomy meaning? If not, why (another meaning, part of a name, used loosely);
- for adaptation and for mitigation: does the term count on its own, need a climate link, or not apply;
- its **role** in the text: climate rationale, system or population, intervention, or result (output, outcome, impact);
- for an intervention or a result: **planned or carried out**, with the words that show it;
- the **links** it sees: climate rationale to intervention, intervention to result, with the passage;
- **taxonomy findings**: climate phrases with no term, terms that seem misclassified, new kinds of climate link.

Every answer carries a quote from the text. Every answer is chosen from a closed list.

<p class="where">In the script: parts <code>schema</code>, <code>prompt</code> (the instructions), <code>client</code> and <code>pipeline</code> (tag_group)</p>

# 5. Checks in code

The AI's answers are never taken on trust. The code checks each one against the text and against the taxonomy. An
answer that fails a check is cancelled and recorded, never repaired by guessing.

- **Quotes**: every quoted passage must be in the text word for word.
- **Candidates**: a tag must be one of the candidates; a word-sense guard blocks known wrong meanings.
- **Stand-alone terms** (standard, Rule 2) count on their own, for the areas the taxonomy gives them.
- **Context-dependent terms** (standard, Rule 3): the code decides the climate link, the same way every time. A general
  term counts for an area when a sentence that holds it also holds climate information of that area: a climate word, a
  stand-alone climate term, or a climate driver said to change ("erratic rainfall"). When the reading (step 6) finds a
  climate measure for the area, every general term of that area in the text counts, because the whole text describes
  climate work. Otherwise only the terms in such a sentence count, so that a passing mention of climate does not make
  the whole text climate-related.
- **Area from the text** (standard, Rule 1 and Table 1): a system, intervention or stakeholder term that the taxonomy
  gives only one area counts for the other area when its own sentence holds climate words specific to that area. "Rice
  production generates significant greenhouse gas emissions" makes Rice count for mitigation.
- **Terms of both areas** (standard, Rule 1): a term classed for both areas counts only for the area the text addresses.
- **Roles**: a role must be one the term's facet allows (a stakeholder cannot be a result).
- **Planned**: kept only with the words that show it ("will develop"); otherwise "unclear".
- **Links** (standard, Rule 5): kept only when both tags count for the area, their roles fit and the passage is in the
  text.

<p class="where">In the script: part <code>validate</code> (validate_record)</p>

# 6. The reading (AI, twice)

For every text with climate information, a stronger model (gpt-5) reads the text **twice, in two independent calls**, and
answers three questions with the exact words of the text (standard, Rule 7):

1. **What kind of work is the result?** A product developed or tested; a product or practice delivered or scaled; a
   training; an event organised; a study of responses; a study of a condition; a policy, plan or recommendation; or other.
2. **What is the climate function of the result**, for adaptation and for mitigation?
   - *specific*: the text says the work addresses a named climate problem, or the product's name states its climate
     function (drought-tolerant variety, early warning system, greenhouse gas inventory);
   - *label*: climate words only qualify a broad goal ("towards climate-resilient food systems", "for climate action");
   - *context*: climate is background, a study variable, one item in a list, a finding, or a name;
   - *none*.
3. **What is the purpose?** Main or additional, by four rules applied in order: the text says main or also; the title
   presents the work by its climate function alone (main) or with other aims (additional); the description names climate
   among other benefits (additional); otherwise not stated.

The code then decides:

- a **climate measure** is a work of a measure kind (not a study of a condition, not "other") with a specific climate
  function. A measure is an intervention of this work with a stated climate function;
- the code refuses a specific function whose words are not in the text or name no climate problem, and a purpose whose
  words are not where its rule says;
- **the two readings are combined**: an area keeps what both support. A measure only when both find one; the purpose
  only when both agree, otherwise "not stated". When the two readings differ, the result is flagged "needs review".

<p class="where">In the script: part <code>prompt</code> (READING_RULES), part <code>validate</code> (apply_reading, use_readings), part <code>pipeline</code> (call_readings)</p>

# 7. Decisions: pathway, level and marker answer

All of this is done by code.

**The climate pathway** (standard, Rules 4 to 6), for adaptation and for mitigation separately, from the tags that count:

| Component | Filled with |
|---|---|
| Climate rationale | climate risk and climate driver terms (drought, climate change, emissions) |
| Geography | the PRMS Countries field, or the countries in the text |
| System or population | system and stakeholder terms (crops, livestock, farmers, communities) |
| Intervention | intervention terms, with their type: the broader term at level 2 of the taxonomy tree |
| Result | output, outcome and impact terms, with their level |

Each relationship is recorded as stated, clear from the context, or not described. Planned and reported information is
kept apart. There is no score.

**The level of each area** (standard, Rule 8):

| Level | What the text shows |
|---|---|
| L0 | No climate information |
| L1 | Climate information, no climate measure |
| L2 | A climate measure; purpose additional or not stated |
| L3 | A climate measure; climate is the main purpose |

**The marker answer** (standard, Rule 9). PRMS has one climate marker for both areas, so it is compared with the stronger
area:

| PRMS marker | L0 | L1 | L2 | L3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Principal | cannot determine | marker higher | cannot determine (purpose not stated); marker higher (additional) | aligned |
| Significant | cannot determine | cannot determine | aligned | marker lower |
| Not targeted | aligned | aligned | marker lower | marker lower |

"Cannot determine" always shows its reason: no climate information, climate context only, or main purpose not stated.
A result with no marker gets "no comparison". The answer is a signal for review; the marker is never changed.

**Review flags** point a reviewer to the results to look at first: the two readings differ, a reading failed, the
countries differ, the text is very short or translated, and others.

<p class="where">In the script: part <code>derive</code> (derive_result, area_level, OUTCOMES)</p>

# 8. Taxonomy findings

Tagging real texts shows where the taxonomy can improve (standard, Rules 10 to 12). Five kinds of finding are collected:

| Finding | Comes from | Proposed action |
|---|---|---|
| Unmatched climate phrase | the AI | add as a synonym of the closest term, or as a new term; reject when there is no climate word |
| Doubtful match | code, from the terms the AI did not keep, with its reason | review that synonym or the definition |
| Possible misclassification | the AI and code | change the term's role, area or facet |
| Unrecorded type of climate anchor | the AI | add an example to the term's context rule |
| Measure with no intervention term | code, after the reading | add a synonym to one of the three closest intervention terms, or propose a new term |

Document 3 lists every finding with its passage, the number of results, the proposed action, the reason and an empty
decision column. Decisions are kept from one run to the next. Nothing enters the taxonomy by itself.

<p class="where">In the script: parts <code>validate</code> (measure_findings), <code>findings</code></p>

# 9. Outputs, running and quality control

**Documents.** Document 1 (tagged results, with sheets for tags and links), document 2 (diagnosis page), document 3
(taxonomy findings), and a run summary with counts and the cost.

**Running.** The script runs one result at a time, in parallel, or through the OpenAI Batch API at half the price. Before
any call it prints a cost estimate, and it stops at a cost cap. The API key is read from the user's settings, never
written in the script.

**Quality control**

- **Fixed test cases**: 46 texts (the standard's worked examples and PRMS cases) with the answers the rules require.
  They run before each tagging run; a blocking failure stops the run.
- **Offline checks**: about 120 checks of the code with written answers in place of the AI, run after every change, at no
  cost.
- **Replay**: the AI's answers are stored, so a change to a rule in code can be replayed on a past run at no cost.
- **Two independent readings** for measure and purpose, with differences flagged.
- **Human double review** on the review site: two reviewers per result, blind until both have answered.

<p class="where">In the script: parts <code>tests</code>, <code>selftest</code>, <code>run</code>, <code>results</code>, <code>outputs</code>; tools <code>offline_checks.R</code>, <code>test_cases.json</code></p>

# Where each rule of the standard is applied

| Rule of the standard | Where it is applied | How |
|---|---|---|
| **1.** Adaptation and mitigation separately | Tagging call; checks in code | One answer per area for each term. Taxonomy area by default; area from the text; terms of both areas count only for the area the text addresses. |
| **2.** Stand-alone terms | Term search; tagging call; checks | The taxonomy role decides; the AI confirms the climate sense; one list of words that look like climate words and are not. |
| **3.** Climate anchors for context-dependent terms | Checks in code, after the reading | A general term counts when its sentence holds climate information; when the work is a climate measure, the text anchors all of them. Names are hidden first. |
| **4.** Pathway components | Decisions | Five components per area from the tags that count, by role; geography from the PRMS Countries field. |
| **5.** Relationships | Tagging call; checks; decisions | Links with a passage, kept when both tags count; recorded as stated, clear from context, or not described. |
| **6.** Type, result level, planned or reported | Taxonomy; tagging call; checks | Type from the taxonomy tree; result level from the role; "planned" only with its words. |
| **7.** Objective, measure, purpose | Reading (gpt-5, twice); checks | Kind of work, climate function, purpose by four rules; what both readings support. |
| **8.** Expectations for each marker | Decisions | Levels L0 to L3. |
| **9.** Alignment or discrepancy | Decisions | The comparison table; the reason shown with "cannot determine"; the marker never changed. |
| **10.** Gaps and errors | Tagging call; checks; findings | Four kinds of finding from the standard and one added: measure with no intervention term. |
| **11.** Synonym or new term | Findings; acronym register | The closest existing term is proposed; a person decides. |
| **12.** Record proposed changes | Findings; outputs | Document 3 with a decision column; the taxonomy version on every record. |

# Words used on this page

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Candidate | A taxonomy term found in the text by the code, which the AI then judges. |
| Stand-alone term | A term that is climate-related by its meaning (drought, early warning system). It counts on its own. |
| Context-dependent term | A general term (irrigation, yield, farmer). It counts only with a climate link in the text. |
| Anchor | The climate information that makes a context-dependent term count. |
| Climate measure | An intervention of this work whose climate function the text states. |
| Purpose | Whether climate is the main or an additional aim of the work, as the text presents it. |
| Level | L0 to L3: how much the text shows, from no climate information to a climate measure with climate as the main purpose. |
| Marker answer | Aligned, marker higher, marker lower, cannot determine, or no comparison. |
| Replay | Running the checks and decisions again on stored AI answers, at no cost. |
